Mountain Province Diamonds sold more than double the diamonds it sold a year ago — and the price it got for each one fell by nearly half.

The Gahcho Kue mine shipped 869,520 carats in the second quarter against 411,114 a year earlier, up 111%. The price per carat fell to CAD 50 from CAD 90, down 44%. The two moves very nearly cancel: revenue rose 18% to CAD 43.5 million, because volume did almost all the lifting a price collapse should have prevented.

The volume came from the plant, not the market. Carats recovered reached just over two million, up 185% — the second straight quarter above that mark. Cash cost fell to CAD 48 a carat recovered, which sits within about CAD 2 of the CAD 50 realised price.

Below the operating line, the quarter reverses. Adjusted EBITDA came in positive at CAD 8.4 million. The net loss was CAD 120.6 million — 2.8 times the quarter's entire revenue, and CAD 129 million below the positive EBITDA line. Only CAD 11.3 million of that gap is disclosed as foreign-exchange loss.

Inside one Indian diamond manufacturer's quarter, the two halves of the business went opposite ways — and the shift explains the margin.

Asian Star reported consolidated revenue of INR 6.47 billion, about $67.7 million, down 11% on the year. Loose-diamond sales fell 22% to INR 4.26 billion. Jewellery revenue rose 17% to INR 2.35 billion. Net profit fell 38% to INR 120.6 million.

Work the percentages backwards and the mix shift is the story: loose stones were about 73% of the two segments combined a year ago and are about 64% now. Nine points of a manufacturer's mix moved out of polishing and into finished goods in four quarters — and the growing segment is the thinner one. Net margin fell to 1.86% from about 2.68% a year ago. The company didn't just sell less. It kept less of what it sold.

One caveat belongs on the arithmetic: the two segment lines sum to INR 6.61 billion against a consolidated INR 6.47 billion, a gap of INR 140 million the company has not itemised.

Two metals on this morning's tape cleared. Two didn't — for the second session running.

Kitco's board at 06:04 New York time read gold $4,393.10, silver $65.00, platinum $1,744.00 and palladium $1,303.00. A second reading on TradingEconomics the same morning: gold $4,394.27, silver $65.124, platinum $1,755.50, palladium $1,322.00. Gold's two pages are 0.027% apart and silver's 0.19% — both inside rounding, both written to this paper's tape as today's marks. Platinum's pages disagree by 0.66% and palladium's by 1.46%. Neither clears, so neither is written: platinum holds $1,749.00 and palladium $1,311.00, both set on 17 August and now two sessions old.

Against yesterday's marks, gold and silver barely moved — gold down 0.03%, silver down 0.58%. The white-metal failure is now a pattern, not a morning: the palladium gap between its two pages roughly doubled over the course of yesterday alone, from 0.69% to 1.46%.
